Vaccine Volunteers

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The race is on to discover a vaccine for COVID-19, who gets there first will determine the fate of billions

Unique Selling Point:
We take you inside the human trials for a COVID-19 vaccine taking place in South Africa

Summary:
It’s been more than 6 months since COVID-19 changed the world. Since then it has infected 16.2 million people world wide and killed almost 650 000 people. The WHO warns that the disease is accelerating at a rapid pace and with no end in sight, it seems that the only way out of this nightmare is to find a vaccine. That’s why Research is happening at breakneck speed. About 140 are in early development, and around two dozen are now being tested on people in clinical trials.



Further information:
It is hoped that a vaccine can be developed as early as the end of 2020. If this indeed is the case, it will the fastest that a vaccine for any disease has ever been discovered. In human history, the previous record is 4 years: that’s how long it took to develop a vaccine for Mumps in the 1960’s

Of the many research projects that are racing to find a vaccine, 3 have proved the most promising:

1. A vaccine developed by Oxford University show it can trigger an immune response. This the the project South Africa is a part of. Human trials are being conducted led by WITS University’s Professor Shabir Madhi
2. Another is China's Sinovac Biotech is starting Phase III trials of its potential coronavirus vaccine in Brazil
3. Then there’s the American Moderna Vaccine which will also plans to start it’s late-stage trial later in July

All 3 use different methodologies to develop its vaccine.

In this story we will focus on the South African study. We will be given full access to the trial and be given an inside look into how the trial is conducted. We will be able to interview the scientists leading the study (interviews with Professor Madhi and his colleagues at Oxford). We will focus of 3 Wits Clinicians who have volunteered to take part in the trial. We will follow their journey through the study, from getting injected with the vaccine to following them in their day-to-day lives, as well as the follow up appointments as their health is tracked through the duration of the study. We’ll also be given access to the locations in which the vaccine trials are taking place and the labs in which samples are analysed

We will also interview representatives of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation to talk about their support for vaccine trials around the world. We will gain a perspective of the mass production of a vaccine learning what it will take to produce a billion vaccines, how long it will take to do this, how much it will cost etc

We’ll talk to other experts about the other vaccine trials taking place and ask the most important questions: When will a vaccine be available for South Africans?

Press Release:


C O V I D-1 9: V A C C I N E T R I A L S
COVID-19: The Human Trials for a Vaccine
With over 20 million confirmed cases worldwide, the coronavirus pandemic is accelerating at a rapid pace and scientists are firmly in the race to find a vaccine. Claiming a “world-first”, this week Russia announced that it was the first country to approve a COVID-19 vaccine. Research for a safe and effective vaccine is happening at breakneck speed and South African scientists have joined the search. Carte Blanche takes you inside the human trials taking place right here at home.
Producer: Julian Sun | Presenter: Derek Watts

Script:


SCRIPT
TEXT: Human trials for a potential COVID-19 vaccine are currently taking place in South Africa. Professor Francois Venter is one of the volunteers…

SOUND Up from Professor Francois Venter on why he chose to be part of COVID-19 Human Vaccine Trials


V/O: It’s been 7 months since COVID-19 changed life as we know it. Currently South Africa has the 5th highest infection rate in the world with over 560 000 cases and 11 000 deaths.

DEREK: With no end in sight, the world is crying out for a vaccine. The billion dollar question is: How soon will one come?





V/O: All around the world, scientists are in a race against time to develop a vaccine.

The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations or CEPI coordinates the development of new vaccines. Dr Melanie Saville is their head of R&D

















V/O:It should take years to develop a vaccine but if scientists are able to discover one for COVID-19 by the end of 2020, it will be the fastest in human history

One of the most promising candidates comes from Oxford University. Professor Andrew Pollard explains how they’ve been able to develop their vaccine so quickly

DEREK: Human trials are crucial when it comes to developing a vaccine and this clinic at Chris Baragwanath Hospital, is one of several sites around South Africa that is testing one of the most promising vaccine candidates in the world

V/O: South African Human trials (which began in July) form part of the Oxford Study and came about because of a personal relationship with WITS University’s Shabir Madhi


Comment from Prof Madhi

Then cut back to Prof Venter saying that Madhi’s unit has extensive experience with vaccine trials and has saved thousands of lives

V/O: This is a phase 2 human trial that will see 2000 volunteers take part. Half will be given the vaccine, the other half a placebo.

The study is double blind, meaning neither scientists or volunteers know which they’re getting.

Prof Venter gives his account of what it’s been like to take part in the trial

V/O: Prof Venter has to return to the clinic for regular checkups. It is one of several test sites around the country as Dr Anthonet Koen explains


V/O: This week, Russian President Vladimir Putin stunned the world when he announced the first ever COVID-19 Vaccine, but doubts remain because phase 3 trials have not been conducted
V/O: The fact remains that no vaccine has been approved by Western regulators. So when will the world and indeed South Africa hope to get one?




V/O: If the Oxford Vaccine proves effective, how much will it cost?
